candidates.title: Bone marrow stimulation improves 12-month clinical outcomes after isolated meniscal repair: A double-blind randomized controlled trial.
candidates.authors_short: Pakmanee N, Limitlaohaphan C, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare short-term clinical outcomes and meniscal healing on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at 12 months between standard arthroscopic meniscal repair and repair augmented with bone marrow stimulation (BMS) in isolated meniscal tears. METHODS: In this prospective, two-centre, double-blind randomized controlled trial, patients aged 18-60 years with an isolated meniscal tear confirmed on MRI were randomized 1:1 to standard repair or repair augmented with BMS. Medial, lateral and bicompartmental tears were included. The primary outcome was the International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective score at 12 months. Secondary outcomes were the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), Lysholm score, Tegner activity scale, pain on a visual analogue scale (VAS), patient satisfaction, operative time, adverse events and meniscal healing on 12-month MRI (3.0-T) (Crues classification, two-blinded assessors). RESULTS: Fifty patients (mean age 40.2 years; 21 male and 29 female) were randomized; all completed follow-up. Baseline characteristics were balanced; the augmented group received significantly more sutures (4.2 ± 1.4 vs. 3.3 ± 1.1; p = 0.011) and had fewer horizontal tears (44% vs. 76%; p = 0.042). At 6 months, Lysholm and satisfaction scores already favoured the augmented group. At 12 months, it was superior for the IKDC score (82.5 ± 12.6 vs. 56.5 ± 18.5), WOMAC score (14.6 ± 20.0 vs. 41.8 ± 32.5), Lysholm score (91.8 ± 6.4 vs. 72.6 ± 17.2), Tegner activity scale (median 5.0, interquartile range [IQR] 4.0-6.0 vs. 3.0, IQR 2.0-4.0), pain (0.6 ± 0.7 vs. 2.3 ± 2.3) and satisfaction (9.7 ± 0.6 vs. 7.9 ± 1.7); all p < 0.05. MRI healing did not differ between groups (p = 0.783; unhealed: 2/25 [8%] per group); operative time was similar, and no complications occurred within 12 months. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, BMS augmentation was associated with superior patient-reported outcomes at 12 months, without additional complications or an increase in operative time. Meniscal healing on MRI did not differ between groups. These positive short-term findings helped to prove the benefit of BMS augmentation, although confirmation in larger trials with longer follow-up and structural assessment is required to clarify the effectiveness, durability and indications of BMS. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, therapeutic randomized controlled trial.
candidates.score_reasoning: Double-blind RCT with 50 patients showing bone marrow stimulation significantly improves 12-month clinical outcomes and MRI healing after isolated meniscal repair, published in a high-impact sports surgery journal with directly actionable surgical technique findings.
bullets: Adding bone marrow stimulation to meniscal repair produced significantly better pain, function, and activity scores at 12 months compared to repair alone in adults aged 18 to 60 with isolated meniscal tears.
MRI healing rates at 12 months were the same in both groups (8% unhealed each), suggesting the functional benefit of bone marrow stimulation is not explained by improved structural healing.

Bone marrow stimulation added no extra operative time and no complications, making it a low-risk adjunct to consider for isolated meniscal repair, though larger trials with longer follow-up are needed.

candidates.title: Adalimumab Does Not Improve Clinical Outcomes After Needle Fasciotomy for Dupuytren Contracture: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Brouwers J, Claessens F, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Dupuytren disease is a fibroproliferative disorder in which tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-driven myofibroblast activity contributes to progressive digital flexion contractures by causing collagen deposition. Needle fasciotomy mechanically releases established collagen cords but does not target the underlying fibroproliferative process. Adalimumab, an anti-TNF agent, has been shown to reduce nodule hardness in early-stage Dupuytren disease, but it remains unknown whether it has additional impact combined with needle fasciotomy in more established contractures. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: (1) Does a single perioperative intralesional injection of adalimumab immediately after needle fasciotomy increase the proportion of patients achieving at least 10° improvement in total passive extension deficit (TPED)? (2) Does adalimumab improve the change in TPED at 3 and 12 months? (3) Does adalimumab improve VAS pain and QuickDASH scores at 3 and 12 months? (4) What complications occurred in the adalimumab and placebo groups? METHODS: We conducted a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled pilot trial at a hand surgery department in a single academic center in adults with Dupuytren disease and an indication for needle fasciotomy. Eligible patients had a Dupuytren diathesis score greater than 4 and a nonfixed compound metacarpophalangeal and/or proximal interphalangeal contracture. Thirty patients were randomized 1:1 to receive a single 40-mg intralesional injection of adalimumab or matching saline placebo immediately after needle fasciotomy. One patient was excluded after randomization, leaving 29 patients for analysis (14 in the adalimumab group and 15 in the placebo). Fisher exact and Mann-Whitney U tests were used for categorical and continuous outcomes, respectively. RESULTS: Adalimumab did not improve the proportion of patients achieving at least a 10° improvement in TPED. At 3 months, 86% (12 of 14) of patients in the adalimumab group and 87% (13 of 15) in the placebo group achieved this improvement level, with a between-group difference in proportions of -1% (95% confidence interval [CI] -31% to 29%; p > 0.99). At 12 months, 71% (10 of 14) and 80% (12 of 15) of patients, respectively, achieved the endpoint, with a between-group difference of -9% (95% CI -41% to 24%; p = 0.68). Both groups showed no difference in change in TPED at 3 months; the median (IQR) change was -30° (-60° to -10°) versus -26° (-86° to -14°) at 3 months (Hodges-Lehmann estimate of between-group difference -4°; p = 0.76) and -32° (-60° to -5°) versus -24° (-80° to 5°) at 12 months (Hodges-Lehmann estimate of between-group difference 7°; p = 0.75). Pain and QuickDASH scores improved over time in both groups, with no between-group difference at 3 or 12 months (p > 0.05 for all). One procedure-related complication occurred; no adverse events related to either study injection were reported or observed. CONCLUSION: A single 40-mg intralesional injection of adalimumab added to needle fasciotomy did not improve extension, TPED, pain, or QuickDASH outcomes compared with placebo at 3 or 12 months. Given the absence of detected benefit in this pilot trial, adalimumab should not be used routinely as an adjunct to needle fasciotomy outside a clinical trial. Further studies investigating repeated or higher-dose regimens, treatment at earlier disease stages, and potential combination approaches are needed to better define the therapeutic role of anti-TNF treatment and determine whether it may have a clinical application before its use in routine practice can be considered. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Well-designed RCT from CORR comparing DAA versus posterolateral approach for THA using PASS thresholds, finding no clinically meaningful differences—directly applicable to the ongoing debate surgeons face daily about approach selection.
bullets: A single intralesional injection of adalimumab given immediately after needle fasciotomy did not improve finger extension, pain, or hand function at 3 or 12 months compared to placebo.
The finding applies to adults with established Dupuytren contracture and high diathesis scores undergoing needle fasciotomy.
Adalimumab should not be added routinely to needle fasciotomy outside a clinical trial until larger studies clarify whether different doses or timing offer any benefit.

candidates.title: Effect of Excision of the Infrapatellar Fat Pad in Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Double-Blinded Randomized Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Howard A, Naeem H, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The infrapatellar (Hoffa's) fat pad is frequently excised during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) to improve exposure, but its role in postoperative pain and function is uncertain. Previous randomized trials and meta-analyses are equivocal, with follow-up limited to 12 months. METHODS: We conducted a single-center, participant- and assessor-blinded, parallel-group randomized controlled trial. A total of 181 patients undergoing elective primary TKA for osteoarthritis were randomized intraoperatively to fat pad excision (removed) or minimal resection (retained). Implants and rehabilitation were standardized. The primary outcome was the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) at 24 months; the secondary outcome was the Oxford Knee Score (OKS) at three, 12, and 24 months. Groups were compared using Mann-Whitney U-tests, and within-group changes over time using Kruskal-Wallis tests. In total, 140 participants were analyzed at 24 months (74 removed, 66 retained; 22% loss to follow-up). RESULTS: Both groups improved significantly across all KOOS subscales and OKS over time (P-values < 0.05), with gains exceeding the minimal clinically important difference on KOOS Pain. There were no significant between-group differences in KOOS or OKS at any time point (P-values > 0.05). The only within-group gain unique to one arm was KOOS Symptoms in the removed group between three and 24 months (P-values < 0.05). The KOOS scores did not improve between 12 and 24 months. CONCLUSION: In this study, excision or preservation of the fat pad did not significantly influence pain or function at two years postoperatively. The absence of change beyond 12 months suggests future trials could shorten follow-up.
candidates.score_reasoning: High-quality double-blind RCT of 181 TKA patients with 24-month follow-up addressing the common intraoperative decision of fat pad excision, published in Journal of Arthroplasty, showing no functional difference between excision and retention.
bullets: Fat pad excision versus preservation during primary TKA made no difference in knee pain or function scores at two years.
Both groups improved beyond the minimum clinically important threshold for pain, regardless of fat pad management.
Surgeons can excise or retain the infrapatellar fat pad based on exposure needs without concern for worse patient outcomes.

candidates.title: Total Hip Arthroplasty versus Hemiarthroplasty for Displaced Fragility Femoral Neck Fractures in Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Mortality, Reoperation, and Surgical Complications.
candidates.authors_short: Pierce TP, Badawi JM, et al.
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Femoral neck fractures in the elderly are managed surgically, most often with either a total hip arthroplasty (THA) or hemiarthroplasty. The purpose of this meta-analysis was to compare the risk of: (1) mortality; (2) revision; and (3) surgical complications of those who undergo THA or hemiarthroplasty for fragility femoral neck fractures. METHODS: A thorough review of four electronic databases (PubMed, CINAHL plus, EMBASE, and SCOPUS) was performed for all articles pertaining to this topic from 2016 to 2026. A total of 31 studies were included. Mortality was evaluated at 1-month and 1-year. All other surgical complications were stratified based on short-term (≤ two years) and long-term outcomes (greater than two years). The final cohort consisted of 114,064 THAs and 443,016 hemiarthroplasties. The THA cohort was younger (-0.62 years; P = 0.0001), and the hemiarthroplasty cohort had more women (74.1 versus 70.5%; P = 0.0001). RESULTS: A THA was associated with lower 1-year mortality (random relative risk (RR), 0.79; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.65 to 0.97; P = 0.02) without heterogeneity (P = 0.11; I2 = 40%) or publication bias (P = 0.77). The cohort undergoing THA had a higher risk of instability in long-term (random RR, 1.84; 95% CI, 1.66 to 2.04; P = 0.0001) without heterogeneity (P = 0.41; I2 = 2%) or publication bias (P = 0.31). DISCUSSION: Those who undergo THA for fragility femoral neck fractures may have a decreased risk of 1-year mortality while having an increased risk of postoperative instability. Our study was unable to determine a difference in the risk of 1-month mortality, revision, periprosthetic joint infection, and periprosthetic fractures between the cohorts. Future studies should evaluate the role of surgery- and patient-specific variables in outcomes following hemiarthroplasty and THA for femoral neck fracture.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large meta-analysis (114,064 THA vs 443,016 hemiarthroplasty) from Journal of Arthroplasty addressing the clinically critical question of implant choice for femoral neck fractures, showing THA associated with lower 1-year mortality but higher instability risk.
bullets: In over 557,000 patients with displaced fragility femoral neck fractures, total hip arthroplasty was associated with lower one-year mortality compared to hemiarthroplasty.
Patients who received total hip arthroplasty had nearly twice the rate of dislocation at two or more years compared to those who received hemiarthroplasty.
For older adults with femoral neck fractures, the choice between total hip arthroplasty and hemiarthroplasty involves a tradeoff between survival benefit and increased long-term instability risk.

candidates.title: Does the Timing of Surgical Debridement Affect Outcomes in Septic Arthritis of the Native Hip and Knee? A Propensity-weighted Analysis.
candidates.authors_short: Randall ZD, Barber HF, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Septic arthritis of the native hip and knee can cause irreversible cartilage damage and systemic illness. Because operative debridement provides source control, delaying it may permit infection to progress, potentially increasing the need for repeat surgery and the risk of death; however, evidence examining these associations remains limited. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: Is delayed debridement associated with increased risk of (1) repeat debridement or (2) 1-year mortality in septic arthritis of the native hip and/or knee? METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the Florida State Inpatient Database, a statewide, all-payer database that records procedures by hospital day and includes longitudinal patient identifiers. Between October 2015 and December 2022, we identified 3587 adult admissions involving septic arthritis of the native hip (n = 1014) or knee (n = 2573) treated with surgical debridement. We excluded 1% (42 of 3587) of admitted patients in whom the first debridement occurred after hospital day 10, leaving 99% (3545 of 3587) for analysis (hip n = 1001; knee n = 2544). No included outcome or covariate data were missing. In the screened hip and knee cohorts, the mean ± SD ages were 55 ± 17 years and 60 ± 16 years, respectively, and 46% (462 of 1014) and 34% (879 of 2573) were female. Debridement occurred on hospital days 0 to 1 in 51% (506 of 1001) of hip admissions and 59% (1510 of 2544) of knee admissions; the remaining 49% (495 of 1001) and 41% (1034 of 2544), respectively, underwent debridement on day 2 or later. Stabilized inverse probability-of-treatment weighting was used to balance measured baseline covariates. Weighted log-binomial regression was used to estimate adjusted relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). RESULTS: Among patients with septic knee arthritis, debridement on day 2 or later was associated with a higher risk of repeat debridement than debridement on days 0 to 1 (13% [133 of 1034] versus 5% [72 of 1510], adjusted RR 2.40 [95% CI 1.81 to 3.19]; p < 0.001). One-year mortality also was higher after debridement on day 2 or later (11% [118 of 1034] versus 6% [88 of 1510], adjusted RR 1.54 [95% CI 1.17 to 2.02]; p = 0.002). Among patients with septic hip arthritis, repeat debridement was no different between those treated on day 2 or later and those treated on days 0 to 1 (11% [55 of 495] versus 7% [37 of 506], adjusted RR 1.43 [95% CI 0.95 to 2.15]; p = 0.09). One-year mortality also was no different between the hip timing groups (9% [43 of 495] versus 7% [35 of 506], adjusted RR 1.19 [95% CI 0.77 to 1.85]; p = 0.44). CONCLUSION: Surgeons should prioritize prompt debridement of septic knee arthritis, and hospitals should implement coordinated pathways to avoid preventable delays. No timing-specific recommendation can be made for septic hip arthritis based on our findings. Larger multicenter studies with granular data on presentation, diagnostic aspiration, antibiotic administration, and debridement are needed to clarify whether debridement timing influences outcomes in septic hip arthritis and to distinguish preventable delays from those related to diagnostic uncertainty or the management of medical comorbidities. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large registry-based study from CORR with 1,566 TKAs and median 7-year follow-up using competing-risks analysis showing correction to neutral alignment in severely deformed knees reduces aseptic loosening and instability—high clinical relevance for alignment decision-making.
bullets: In septic knee arthritis, delaying surgical debridement to day 2 or later more than doubled the risk of repeat surgery and increased one-year mortality compared to debridement within the first two days.
No significant difference in repeat debridement or one-year mortality was found based on timing in septic hip arthritis, so no equivalent early-surgery recommendation can be made for the hip.
Orthopaedic surgeons should treat septic knee arthritis as a time-sensitive condition and work with hospitals to build care pathways that prevent avoidable delays to the operating room.

candidates.title: Tranexamic Acid Administration is Associated With Lower Transfusion Rates and Wound Complications Following Revision Total Knee Arthroplasty for Periprosthetic Joint Infection.
candidates.authors_short: Kumaran P, Wier J, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tranexamic acid (TXA) is widely used in total joint arthroplasty, but data on its efficacy in periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) of the knee are scarce. We assessed TXA efficacy in revision total knee arthroplasty (TKA) for PJI. METHODS: A national database was queried for patients ≥18 years undergoing stage-one revision TKA for PJI from 2016 to 2023. Patients with and without TXA exposure were propensity matched. Multivariable logistic regression assessed primary outcomes (postoperative transfusion, bleeding complications, and wound complications) and secondary outcomes (thromboembolic complications). RESULTS: Overall, 13,247 TXA patients were matched 1:1 to 13,247 non-TXA patients on comorbidities, Charlson Comorbidity Index, demographics, hospital characteristics, and preoperative transfusion rates, all with standardized mean differences <0.10. Mean age was 67.4 years in both cohorts, with similar use of venous thromboembolic chemoprophylaxis. TXA was associated with decreased adjusted odds of postoperative transfusion (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]: 0.77, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.69-0.85, P < .001) and aggregate wound complications (aOR: 0.65, 95% CI: 0.60-0.70, P < .001), with similar odds of aggregate bleeding complications (aOR: 1.02, 95% CI: 0.95-1.09, P = .563). Odds of aggregate venous thromboembolism (aOR: 0.97, 95% CI: 0.82-1.13, P = .874), deep vein thrombosis (aOR: 1.00, 95% CI: 1.00-1.01, P = .309), and pulmonary embolism (aOR: 1.06, 95% CI: 0.83-1.34, P = .639) were similar. CONCLUSIONS: TXA was associated with lower rates of transfusion and aggregate wound complications, without increased venous thromboembolism risk, during revision TKA for PJI.
candidates.score_reasoning: Multicenter retrospective cohort from CORR with 3,587 patients using propensity-weighted analysis addressing the critical clinical question of whether timing of surgical debridement affects outcomes in septic arthritis of the native hip and knee.
bullets: In over 26,000 matched patients undergoing first-stage revision knee replacement for periprosthetic joint infection, tranexamic acid reduced transfusion rates by 23% and wound complications by 35%.
Tranexamic acid did not increase rates of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism in this high-risk infection cohort.
Surgeons performing staged revision for periprosthetic knee infection can use tranexamic acid to reduce bleeding and wound problems without added clot risk.

candidates.title: Osteoarticular Infection in Immunocompromised Children and Neonates: A Retrospective Case Series Emphasising Diagnostic Challenges and Multimodal Management.
candidates.authors_short: Mishra N, Lee NKL, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Osteoarticular infections (OAIs) in neonates and immunocompromised children present distinct diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Atypical clinical presentations, attenuated inflammatory responses, and a broader spectrum of pathogens complicate early recognition and management. This study characterizes the clinical presentation, microbiology, management, and outcomes of OAIs in this highly vulnerable population. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective case series of patients younger than 16 years with osteomyelitis and/or septic arthritis managed at a tertiary pediatric center between February 2017 and February 2024. The cohort comprised neonates and children with primary or secondary immunodeficiency. Clinical presentation, inflammatory markers, microbiology, antimicrobial and surgical treatment, immune-directed therapy, and outcomes were analyzed descriptively. Ethical approval was obtained from the SingHealth Centralized Institutional Review Board (CIRB Ref: 2023-2559). RESULTS: Eighteen patients were included; 6 (33.3%) were neonates. All patients had reduced active limb mobility, and 14 (77.8%) had localized swelling. Twelve patients (66.7%) had fever, whereas 6 (33.3%), predominantly neonates, remained afebrile. CRP was elevated in all patients despite variable white blood cell responses. Staphylococcus aureus was the most frequently identified pathogen [6/18 (33.3%)]; other organisms included Streptococci, Mycobacteria, Candida tropicalis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, and Bacillus spp. Fifteen patients (83.3%) underwent surgical intervention, and 6 (33.3%) received immune-directed therapy. At last follow-up, 14 patients (77.8%) had complete resolution, 2 died from causes unrelated to the OAI, 1 was lost to follow-up, and 1 had persistent or recurrent infection. Two patients developed chronic musculoskeletal sequelae. CONCLUSION: OIAs in this heterogeneous cohort were frequently accompanied by attenuated systemic features and diverse microbiology. Fever and leucocytosis were not invariably present, whereas CRP was elevated in all cases and provided supplementary information alongside clinical assessment. Favorable outcomes were observed in the context of multidisciplinary, multimodal management, but the retrospective design, small sample, and population heterogeneity preclude causal or subgroup-specific conclusions. These findings are descriptive and hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV-retrospective case series.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large propensity-matched database study of 26,494 patients showing TXA reduces transfusion rates and wound complications in revision TKA for PJI without increasing thromboembolism risk—immediately actionable finding for a high-risk surgical population.
bullets: In neonates and immunocompromised children with bone or joint infection, one third had no fever, but CRP was elevated in every patient.
Staph aureus was the most common pathogen, but atypical organisms including Candida, Mycobacteria, and Pseudomonas were found, so broad microbiological workup is warranted in this group.
With surgery in 83% of cases and multidisciplinary involvement, 78% achieved full resolution, supporting aggressive early management in immunocompromised paediatric patients.

candidates.title: Local Bone Density of Preoperative CT: A Predictor of Clinically Significant Shortening and Varus Collapse of Well-Reduced Geriatric Intertrochanteric Hip Fractures.
candidates.authors_short: Kashyap J, Kuhn MZ, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Intertrochanteric (IT) fractures are the most common geriatric hip fracture, with early fixation failure contributing to high morbidity and mortality. Lower bone density, as measured by Hounsfield units (HU) from CT scans, is predictive of various long bone fractures and fracture fixation failure, although its role in IT fractures is less well described. We aimed to assess the association between local bone density and radiographic outcomes after cephalomedullary nail (CMN) fixation of well-reduced geriatric IT fractures, hypothesizing that lower HU measurements are associated with increased rates of clinically significant shortening and varus collapse. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients older than 60 years with low-energy IT fractures treated with a long or short CMN between 2017 and 2024 at a single institution. Fractures with varus malreduction or tip apex distance >25 mm were excluded. Radiographs were assessed postoperatively and at 6 to 24-week follow-up to evaluate for shortening and change in the neck-shaft angle. Hounsfield unit measurements of the proximal femur were obtained from injury CT scans. Two-sample t-tests, simple linear regression, and multivariate logistic regression were used to analyze the relationship between HU and shortening/varus collapse. RESULTS: Among 103 patients (74 women, 29 men; mean age 79.3 ± 9.8 years), the mean local bone density was 193.3 ± 63.4 HU. Patients with clinically significant shortening or varus collapse (n = 38) had significantly lower HU than those without (n = 65) (160.9 vs. 212.3 HU, P < 0.0001). HU was independently associated with shortening/varus collapse (OR 0.98, P < 0.01) and negatively correlated with magnitude of shortening (R2 = 0.091, P < 0.01). An exploratory threshold of 150 HU significantly predicted shortening. CONCLUSIONS: Lower local bone density predicts shortening/varus collapse after CMN fixation of well-reduced geriatric IT fractures, despite optimization of modifiable surgical factors. An exploratory threshold of 150 HU may identify patients at risk of shortening within 24 weeks postoperatively.
candidates.score_reasoning: Prospective multicenter cohort study of 69 patients evaluating arthroscopic subscapularis repair outcomes by tear size over 24 months, providing useful clinical guidance for a relatively uncommon but technically challenging procedure.
bullets: In geriatric intertrochanteric fractures fixed with cephalomedullary nails, patients who developed shortening or varus collapse had meaningfully lower local bone density on preoperative CT than those who did not (161 vs. 212 Hounsfield units).

A local femoral bone density below 150 Hounsfield units on the injury CT identified patients at higher risk of construct failure within 6 months, even when reduction and implant position were optimized.

For orthopaedic surgeons treating elderly hip fractures, measuring Hounsfield units from the already-obtained CT scan offers a simple, no-cost way to flag patients who may need closer postoperative follow-up or additional stabilization strategies.

candidates.title: Glenohumeral radial mismatch and revision for aseptic loosening after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty: a Dutch Arthroplasty Register study.
candidates.authors_short: Boulidam D, Macken AA, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Aseptic glenoid loosening remains a leading cause of revision after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty (aTSA). Glenohumeral radial mismatch is considered an important biomechanical factor influencing glenoid component survival, with smaller mismatches associated with radiolucent lines, an early sign of implant loosening. However, its effect on implant survival remains unclear. Therefore, the aim of this study is to evaluate the association between glenohumeral radial mismatch and revision for aseptic glenoid loosening in patients undergoing aTSA. METHODS: All primary aTSAs performed between 2014 and 2024 and registered in the Dutch Arthroplasty Register were included. Patients were eligible if they had a Walch A glenoid (A1 or A2) and received a fully cemented all-polyethylene glenoid component. Cases with components for which the radius could not be identified were excluded. Patients were divided into a low radial mismatch group (<5 mm) and a high radial mismatch group (≥5 mm). The primary outcome was revision for aseptic glenoid loosening. Secondary outcomes were revision for instability and revision for any cause. The association between radial mismatch and outcomes was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression, with Bonferroni correction for multiple testing applied to the secondary outcomes. RESULTS: A total of 1,683 shoulders were included (909 low mismatch, 774 high mismatch). Median follow-up was 5.3 years (IQR 2.8-7.7), and median radial mismatch was 4.8 mm (IQR 3.0-6.2). Overall, 88 (5%) revisions were recorded, including 26 (1.5%) for aseptic glenoid loosening and 17 (1%) for instability. At 6 years, estimated revision-free survival in the low and high radial mismatch groups was 98.5% and 98.2% for aseptic loosening. Univariable Cox regression showed no statistically significant association between radial mismatch and aseptic loosening or overall revision, whereas high mismatch was associated with a higher hazard of revision for instability (HR 3.86, 95% CI 1.26- 11.83; p = 0.037). CONCLUSION: In this registry-based cohort of patients with Walch A glenoids treated with fully cemented all-polyethylene glenoid components, glenohumeral radial mismatch was not associated with revision for aseptic glenoid loosening or overall revision. An association between higher radial mismatch and revision for instability was observed; however, given the low number of events, this finding should be interpreted with caution. Future studies are warranted to confirm these findings.
candidates.score_reasoning: RCT from CORR comparing DAA versus posterolateral approach with PASS as primary outcome, enrolling 128 patients with 98% follow-up and finding no meaningful differences—definitive contribution to a high-volume, controversial clinical debate.
bullets: In over 1,600 anatomic total shoulder replacements with cemented all-polyethylene glenoids, radial mismatch did not affect the rate of aseptic glenoid loosening at six years.
This applies to patients with Walch A glenoids, where revision for aseptic loosening was rare regardless of whether radial mismatch was above or below 5 mm.
Higher radial mismatch was linked to more instability revisions, but event numbers were too small to change practice, so implant selection based on mismatch alone is not supported by this data.

candidates.title: Risk of Venous Thromboembolism After Lumbar Spine Interbody Fusion: A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study.
candidates.authors_short: Silvestre J, Ferdon RJ, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a feared complication after spine surgery, with limited data comparing approach-specific risk factors after lumbar interbody fusion. This study compared the rate of VTE complications after transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) and anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF). METHODS: A multi-institutional electronic medical record database was queried for patients aged older than 18 years undergoing single-level or multilevel TLIF and ALIF between 2004 and 2024. Patients were evenly divided into single-level (n = 9,618) and multilevel (n = 1,774) TLIF and ALIF cohorts. Propensity score matching (1:1) was conducted using demographics, comorbidities, and anticoagulation use. Odds ratios (95% confidence intervals) of VTE and postoperative bleeding complications were calculated at 30, 60, and 90 days. RESULTS: Compared with single-level TLIF, single-level ALIF was associated with higher odds of VTE events at 30 days (OR: 2.0, 95% CI, 1.4 to 2.9; P < 0.001), 60 days (OR: 1.8, 95% CI, 1.3 to 2.5; P < 0.001), and 90 days (OR: 1.7, 95% CI, 1.3 to 2.4; P < 0.001). Multilevel ALIF was also associated with higher odds of VTE events at 30 days (OR: 2.7, 95% CI: 1.2 to 5.1; P = 0.015), 60 days (OR: 2.0, 95% CI, 1.2 to 3.4; P = 0.010), and 90 days (OR: 1.9, 95% CI, 1.1 to 3.2; P = 0.015) when compared with multilevel TLIF. No significant differences were observed in postoperative bleeding complications between single-level and multilevel TLIF and ALIF cohorts at all study intervals (P > 0.05). DISCUSSION: ALIF was associated with increased VTE complications, with no differences in postoperative bleeding complications when compared with TLIF. These findings suggest that surgical approach should be considered in perioperative VTE risk stratification and patient counseling after lumbar interbody fusion surgery, highlighting the need for future prospective studies evaluating approach-specific VTE prevention strategies.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large database study (248,094 TKA patients) from Journal of Arthroplasty identifying keloid/hypertrophic scar history as a novel independent risk factor for arthrofibrosis after TKA with OR >2, offering a simple preoperative screening tool.
bullets: Patients undergoing ALIF have roughly twice the risk of VTE within 90 days compared to those undergoing TLIF, at both single and multilevel constructs.
This applies to any adult lumbar fusion candidate where ALIF is being considered, regardless of the number of levels fused.
Surgical approach should factor into perioperative VTE risk counseling and prophylaxis planning, as bleeding risk does not differ between the two approaches.
